item.title: Move Over Week Begins, a Senator Recovers, and Ellison Comes Home to Bard
item.description:
Move Over Week Begins, a Senator Recovers, and Ellison Comes Home to Bard. Hosted by Noel.
Monday, November 2, 2026, midday. New York State Police begin a five-day Move Over Law enforcement campaign today, running through Friday, November 6, as part of Crash Responder Safety Week, in partnership with the state Department of Transportation and the Thruway Authority, as reported in June Mercer's RFTUV blotter. A March 27, 2024 expansion extended the law to any vehicle parked, stopped, or standing on the shoulder or elsewhere on a parkway or controlled-access highway, including a disabled car with a flat tire or mechanical trouble, even when no emergency responder is present; the driver guidance is to slow down and move over a lane if safe, or slow down and pass cautiously if a lane change is not safe. Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy, 53, is recovering in hospital after a stroke: his office says he felt numbness in his arm at his son's hockey game on Saturday, October 31, was found at a local hospital to have had a stroke, and was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring, where he is responding well to treatment; his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said Sunday that doctors are encouraged by his progress, that he is awake and alert, and that his office is optimistic he will make a full recovery. He is not on the midterm ballot. In Annandale-on-Hudson, Bard College has opened the Ralph Ellison Center, on the campus where Ellison taught American and Russian literature from 1958 to 1961; a $3.6 million donation from the Ralph and Fanny Ellison Charitable Trust made the center possible, and Bard now holds all the intellectual rights, copyrights, and royalties from his works, including Invisible Man (1952), while the Ellison archive remains at the Library of Congress and will be digitized by the center; programs include the biannual Ralph Ellison Lectures, artist and writer residencies, a 10-week archival internship with partner HBCUs, and a yearlong commemoration of Invisible Man planned for its 75th anniversary in 2027. The local close covers Election Day tomorrow, Tuesday, November 3, with polls open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., no early voting today, the Attorney General's Election Protection Hotline at (866) 390-2992, and a mild, mostly sunny Monday in the Hudson Valley with the next chance of rain late in the week. Hosted by Noel.
Stories: - Move Over enforcement week starts today in New York (RFTUV blotter; 518News as cited) - Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy suffers a stroke and is recovering in hospital (USA TODAY; Associated Press; statement of his office) - Ralph Ellison's works have a new home at Bard College (Associated Press; Bard College announcement) - Election Day is tomorrow, and a mild Monday (RFTUV blotter; Weather Channel)

item.title: The Binance Heist, Who Pays When Agents Read, and Three Peekskill Arrests
item.description:
The Binance Heist, Who Pays When Agents Read, and Three Peekskill Arrests. Hosted by Noel.
Sunday, November 1, 2026, evening. More than $6 billion in virtual assets was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, on Thursday, October 29; the New York Post estimates $6.3 billion, the largest crypto heist in history, taken in about 20 minutes through multiple breach points including an engineer's computer. The FBI said Saturday that North Korea was responsible and that the group TraderTraitor carried out the theft, the same group blamed for the $1.5 billion Bybit theft in February 2025; the bureau says the actors are converting the assets into Ethereum and urges companies to block transactions tied to the laundering addresses. President Trump cast doubt on North Korea's involvement on Saturday. Binance has set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds, says it will fully cover the impact, and had replenished 90 percent of the stolen funds by Saturday; withdrawals, suspended after the attack, resumed in phases on Sunday, with $4.65 billion withdrawn and $1.01 billion deposited by mid-afternoon GMT. The Post's "Black October" framing, a month of AI-enhanced hacking, is carried as that paper's reporting and its experts' concern; the FBI has not said AI carried out this theft. In Forbes, Aaron Stanley asks who pays when AI agents read content online: video platforms and ad-supported publishers earn from human attention an agent never gives them, Rumble's Glenn Rothwell says agents could come to account for most of Rumble's consumption, and Tempo and Stripe's Machine Payments Protocol would let agents pay per use, by card or stablecoin, with bar-tab style sessions settling sub-cent charges; the author notes this solves collection, not valuation, not the author's share, and not the risk to subscriptions. In Peekskill, Westchester County Police say Omar Travis, 59, Rodney Jones, 57, and Kristopher Gaffney, 57, were arrested Thursday after a search at a home on Highland Avenue ended a three-month investigation into suspected narcotics activity at the Dunbar Heights complex; police say the search found six ounces of cocaine, 34 grams of oxycodone, multiple rounds of ammunition, and drug paraphernalia, with no firearm reported found. Travis and Jones are each charged with second-degree and third-degree criminal possession of a controlled substance; Gaffney is charged with tampering with physical evidence. The charges are accusations, not convictions, and no arraignment information has been published. The local close covers the Hudson Valley Renegades and Heritage Financial Credit Union fourth annual Veterans Day Food Drive, collecting non-perishable food through November 11 for the Castle Point VA Medical Center in Wappingers Falls, with drop-offs at Heritage Financial Park, 1500 NY-9D, Wappingers Falls, and the Heritage Financial Credit Union branch at 1476 NY-9D, Wappingers Falls; Dutchess County's animal cruelty hotline, live today around the clock at (845) 867-5055 for non-emergency reports (call 911 for an emergency involving an animal); and the end of early voting in Dutchess County today, with Election Day on Tuesday, November 3. Hosted by Noel.
Stories: - The Binance theft is confirmed, and withdrawals have resumed (AFP via TechXplore; New York Post; FBI statement as quoted by AFP) - When AI agents read content online, who pays? (Forbes) - Three Peekskill men arrested after a three-month narcotics investigation (News 12 Hudson Valley) - A food drive for veterans, a hotline's first day, and the polls ahead (Hudson Valley Renegades; RFTUV)

item.description:
Red Hook Eats New York, Flock Cameras Face a Cover Deadline, and a Pipeline Sentence. Hosted by Noel.
Sunday, November 1, 2026, midday. Red Hook Central School District begins New York November today, its third year of sourcing every fruit, vegetable, and protein on school lunch trays from New York producers, several in the Hudson Valley, run by Food Service Director Sam Pride. The month's landmarks: a November 5 kickoff menu designed by Culinary Institute of America (Hyde Park) students, New York Pizza Palooza every Friday, a first in-house pork roast on November 19, and a Thanksgiving meal on November 24. item.title: A Personal Agent in the Pentagon, a Compute Limit in Albany, and Flu Six Weeks Early
item.description:

WIRED reported on October 29, citing sources, that an Accenture contractor connected a personal Claude Code account to a production environment on NIPRNet, the Defense Department's unclassified network, which holds Controlled Unclassified Information and serves multiple intelligence agencies. WIRED reported no indication that classified systems were accessed and does not establish that a known weakness in that service was exploited. Accenture told WIRED the allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit and that it complied with its legal and contractual obligations; the Defense Department declined to comment. Plus: State Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Jordan Wright introduced a bill expanding the RAISE Act that would let New York limit computing power for risky AI models, covering companies spending more than $1 billion on AI development over three years, with quarterly reporting, 90-day risk assessments, annual audits, and penalties up to $1 million per day for a first violation and $3 million per day for later violations. It is a proposal, not a law. And influenza is prevalent and widespread in New York about six weeks ahead of schedule, with 3,526 laboratory-confirmed cases in the week ending October 17, up 19 percent and about 400 percent above the same period last year, and Orange, Putnam, Westchester, and Sullivan among the highest-count counties. item.title: The Mac Permission Slip, the $6 Trillion Test, and the Trust Gap
item.description:
The RFTUV Briefing for October 3, 2026. Three stories today.
Apple is rewriting Mac Full Disk Access because of AI agents. What the new explicit permission means, and how to check which apps already have access on your Mac.
Bain and Company says the AI buildout needs about $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031. Existing AI markets may supply $1.2 to $1.8 trillion of that. Where the rest is supposed to come from, and why it matters for prices and product durability.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll finds 73 percent of Americans worry AI companies have not gone far enough to prevent serious harm, as a new White House voluntary accord asks six companies to police themselves with audits and board committees.
What changed, why it matters, and what to watch next. Full articles at rftuv.ai.
